name: persistent pulmonary hypertension
aliases: persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

clinicalPearls: Results from failure of the normal fall in pulmonary vascular resistance at birth, sustaining foetal-pattern right-to-left shunting across the patent foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus.
Occurs mainly in term and near-term neonates and presents with cyanosis and hypoxaemia that is disproportionate to any parenchymal lung disease and often strikingly labile.
A pre- to post-ductal oxygen saturation gradient (right hand higher than lower limb, typically by more than 5 to 10 percent) suggests right-to-left ductal shunting.

Common precipitants include meconium aspiration syndrome, sepsis or pneumonia, congenital diaphragmatic hernia, respiratory distress syndrome, perinatal asphyxia, and idiopathic (maldeveloped vasculature) disease.
Echocardiography is essential to confirm raised pulmonary pressures, define shunt direction and, critically, exclude structural congenital heart disease.
Supportive care is foundational: optimise lung recruitment and oxygenation, correct acidosis, avoid hypothermia and agitation, and maintain systemic blood pressure to limit right-to-left shunting.
Inhaled nitric oxide is the first-line selective pulmonary vasodilator, with agents such as sildenafil used as adjuncts.
Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation is the rescue therapy when maximal medical management fails, with the oxygenation index guiding escalation.
reference.pathophysiology: At birth, lung aeration and rising oxygen tension normally trigger pulmonary vasodilatation and a rapid fall in pulmonary vascular resistance. In PPHN this transition fails or reverses through one of three mechanisms: maladaptation (structurally normal vasculature with abnormal vasoconstriction driven by asphyxia, sepsis or acidosis), maldevelopment (remodelled, abnormally muscularised arteries following chronic intrauterine stress), or hypoplasia (a reduced cross-sectional vascular bed, as in congenital diaphragmatic hernia). Persistently high pulmonary vascular resistance maintains right-to-left shunting across the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus, bypassing the lungs and causing severe hypoxaemia. Hypoxaemia and acidosis further raise pulmonary vascular resistance, creating a self-perpetuating cycle.
additionalDifferentials: Cyanotic congenital heart disease (transposition of the great arteries, total anomalous pulmonary venous return, hypoplastic left heart)
Neonatal sepsis or pneumonia (group B streptococcus)
Respiratory distress syndrome from surfactant deficiency
additionalInvestigations: Pre- and post-ductal pulse oximetry to detect differential saturations
Echocardiography with Doppler (shunt direction, tricuspid regurgitation jet, exclusion of structural disease)
Arterial blood gas with calculation of the oxygenation index
Sepsis screen including blood cultures, full blood count and inflammatory markers
Hyperoxia test to help distinguish from cyanotic congenital heart disease
redFlags: Severe labile hypoxaemia refractory to high inspired oxygen
Rising oxygenation index despite maximal support, prompting ECMO consideration
Suspicion of duct-dependent congenital heart disease
reference.prognosis: With inhaled nitric oxide and ECMO the majority of infants survive, but PPHN still carries appreciable mortality and a risk of long-term neurodevelopmental and sensorineural hearing impairment, so structured follow-up is warranted.
pitfalls: Failing to exclude cyanotic congenital heart disease before attributing hypoxaemia to PPHN.
Giving inhaled nitric oxide in duct-dependent lesions or before echocardiography.
Excessive handling, agitation and hypothermia, all of which worsen pulmonary vasoconstriction.
Over-aggressive hyperventilation and induced alkalosis, which are associated with adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes.
Overlooking the pre- to post-ductal saturation gradient.
